title: How Grief Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss human grief. They open with the phrase "good grief" and a story about Domini, an elderly elephant at the Prince of Wales Zoo in Lucknow, India, who grieved and died after her pregnant companion Chumpacali died in childbirth. They debate whether animals truly grieve, citing a chimpanzee carrying her dead baby. They then cover anticipatory, unanticipated, and ambiguous grief; Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's five stages (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) and the W-shaped and day-to-day oscillation of grief; recent studies of widows and widowers and the duration of grief; the DSM-5 proposal to remove the bereavement exclusion for depression; coping advice (avoid alcohol, eat right, exercise, memorial projects, letters, therapy); complicated grief and its risk factors; the difference between grief and trauma; pet loss; and Victorian grief customs and bereavement photography. The episode closes with a listener mail/administrative details segment thanking listeners for gifts and postcards.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and the phrase 'good grief'
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the phrase 'good grief' and its possible origin as a minced oath, and set up the episode as being about human grief.

segments.title: Elephant Domini grieves for Chumpacali
segments.summary: The hosts recount how Domini, a 72-year-old elephant at the Prince of Wales Zoo in Lucknow, India, bonded with pregnant elephant Chumpacali, who died in childbirth with a stillborn calf. Domini wept, stopped eating and drinking, and died a few days later despite veterinary treatment. Josh shares a story about his childhood dog.

segments.title: Do animals grieve?
segments.summary: The hosts note scientists are divided on whether animals grieve. They discuss a chimpanzee who carried her dead baby for days, which some scientists interpret as an adaptive response rather than grief, and they contrast animal behavior with human funeral practices.

segments.title: Grief is personal; a man dies on the way to his wife's funeral
segments.summary: The hosts describe a man who died in a limousine on the way to his wife's funeral after 62 years of marriage, and his daughters holding a double funeral. They conclude there is no set way grief works and that it is a very personal experience.

segments.title: Types of grief: anticipatory, unanticipated, ambiguous
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck describe anticipatory grief, which can be easier because it develops over time, unanticipated grief from sudden events, and ambiguous grief where there is no closure, such as a kidnapping or abandonment. They note grief need not come from death, and define grief and bereavement.

segments.title: Kübler-Ross's five stages of grief
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's 1969 five stages of grief (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance) and their skepticism about whether the stages are universal. Chuck and Josh share personal reactions to a friend's death.

segments.title: Stages as a W curve; day-to-day oscillation; duration of grief
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a chart describing grief as a W shape and recent studies of widows and widowers showing day-to-day swings. Recovery is said to take roughly six months to three years for most people, with the hosts noting such ranges are generalizations. They also discuss the DSM-5 proposal to remove the bereavement exclusion for depression diagnoses.

segments.title: Coping advice and memorial projects
segments.summary: The hosts discuss healthy coping: avoiding drugs and alcohol, eating right, exercising, writing letters to the deceased, making memorials or video tributes, and throwing oneself into projects or organizations the deceased would have appreciated, such as MADD.

segments.title: G.G. Allin funeral aside
segments.summary: A brief tangent in which the hosts discuss the unusual funeral of punk performer GG Allin and his stage persona and death.

segments.title: Therapy, grief statistics, and relief after a spouse's death
segments.summary: The hosts say many people go to therapy, but it is not helpful for everyone, and that significant grief affects a fairly small share of bereaved people in several studies. One study found ten percent of people who lost a spouse felt relief, typically those unhappy in their marriage. They also mention a finding that men may grieve more heavily.

segments.title: Complicated grief and grief versus trauma
segments.summary: The hosts describe complicated grief, when life is disrupted for months, and how counselors may approach it differently. They list risk factors, including death of a child, sudden or traumatic death, and close co-dependence, and distinguish grief from trauma, such as traumatizing dreams about oneself being endangered.

segments.title: Grieving the loss of a pet
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the loss of a pet can be as painful as losing a family member for some people, and advise talking with others who share those feelings rather than people who dismiss pet loss.

segments.title: Victorian grief customs and bereavement photography
segments.summary: Chuck describes research by Paul Rosenblatt on Victorian diaries, in which mourners tried to keep the dead present and grief was expected to last a lifetime. Victorian customs included wearing black for a year and bereavement photography. A listener emailed about a cast of a baby's hands and feet given by a hospital.

segments.title: Closing remarks and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the grief topic, suggest searching the HowStuffWorks site for more, and sign off.
